notes: \cpara{Sun Tzu's advice to leave a besieged enemy a way out. The wording is not Giles's (1910), which reads ``When you surround an army, leave an outlet free.'' The commentators Giles quotes give the purpose: to keep the enemy from ``fighting with the courage of despair.'' The post applies the same purpose to oneself.}
\cpara{A line from Bujold's novel \textsc{Komarr} (1998). I could not check it against the book.}
\cpara{The occasion: at a rationalists' gathering, a woman says she rejects cryonics because the soul would not stay with the frozen body, and the author asks how she knows.}
\cpara{Infers from one look on her face that the question ``had never occurred to her,'' hedged with ``pretty clear,'' and adds that this is no criticism of her.}
\cpara{Says most of the talk covered earlier posts, and introduces the one new notion.}

\cpara{The technique, given as advice to her: accept the feared premise, picture its consequences and what you would do, and do this before weighing the evidence. The two sample thoughts answer her objection (cryonics) and the theist's (morality).}

\cpara{States the principle through Sun Tzu, with the example of a feared layoff. The advice is old as a remedy for fear. Seneca's 24th letter tells a friend facing a lawsuit to ``assume that what you fear may happen will certainly happen in any event'' and to ``measure it in your own mind, and estimate the amount of your fear'' (Gummere's translation). What the post adds is the purpose: to lower the fear so as to judge the probability ``fairly.'' It names no precedent.}
\cpara{Gives the mechanism, and calls it ``the hope'': imagining takes less courage than estimating, and makes estimating easier. No evidence is offered for either step.}
\cpara{Adds that visualizing a scary belief is not conceding it, and that an unthinkable thought controls you even if it is false.}
\cfact{The quoted sentence is the author's own, from the second virtue of ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' (2006). The post does not say so.}
\cpara{Transition: the technique needs some self-honesty.}

\cpara{The easier test: admitting which ideas scare you. As support, the post offers the author's own use of the technique (``Does it help if I say that I have occasion to use this technique myself?''), with no case described.}
\cpara{The harder test: accepting the premise for real and working out how you would deal with it, against the first impulse to find reasons it cannot be so.}

\cpara{Uses the theist who says morality is impossible without God to show how hard honest visualization is. The claim the paragraph answers is a forecast of conduct: ``they wouldn't go around slaughtering babies.''}

\clogic{The paragraph answers the claim as a forecast of conduct, which fits the conversation the footnote describes. Philosophers usually mean something else by the same words: that without God nothing would be objectively right or wrong. Some non-believers have accepted a version of that claim; the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (``Moral Arguments for the Existence of God'') names Mackie and Nietzsche as allies theists can enlist ``in arguing that God is necessary for objective morality.'' Picturing one's own conduct does not bear on that version, and the post does not claim it does.}
\cpara{Adds that people get over things, with quadriplegics as the example, so you would come to terms with a feared truth too.}

\cfact{Given without a source. Research supports the direction: a review by Ubel, Loewenstein and Jepson (2003) reports that patients often rate their quality of life higher than the public rates the same conditions, and lists unforeseen adaptation as one possible cause. It also finds the adaptation partial. In two national panels, the onset of a long-term disability brought ``moderate to large drops in happiness \ldots\ followed by little adaptation over time'' (Lucas, 2007). ``People do get over things'' holds only in part.}

\cpara{Points to the Litanies of Gendlin and Tarski and restates Gendlin: ``owning up to it doesn't make it worse.'' For the limits of that claim, see the notes on ``You Can Face Reality.'' The narrower claim that follows, that picturing a world does no harm either way, is about imagining, not learning, and that objection does not apply to it.}
\cpara{A rhetorical question that implies few would keep their belief. No evidence is given.}
\cpara{Concludes that the technique is ``powerful'' but takes effort. ``Powerful'' is asserted. The conversation that opened the post is left without an outcome.}
